summary:
Gujarat stands under the national framework of India, and the source inventory records no Gujarat-specific legal or enforcement deviation material enough to distinguish this state from the national baseline. A visitor therefore faces the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, passed by the Parliament of India in March 2026, which replaces the 2019 Act's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals. Self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people fall outside the recognition scheme, and the amendment mandates medical certification for identity recognition, so document practice for a trans traveller rests on that certification.

The amendment removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court of India's 2014 judgment recognising a third gender. Human Rights Watch described the bill as a major setback that strips thousands of rights and increases risk. The government presents the change as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. At the time of reporting in March 2026 the bill had cleared both houses of Parliament and awaited presidential assent.

Entry and stay rest on a mixed baseline. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped openly transgender law student Sakshi Jain although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination, with the Allahabad High Court granting relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.
tangentialFactors:
The March 2026 amendment drew protests from opposition parties and from the LGBTQ community, and rights activists including Akkai Padmashali describe it as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government's stated rationale, wider access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, stands against the critics' finding that the redefinition excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people.

The direction of travel in statute and in the courts diverges. Recognition narrowed in March 2026 and sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, while high courts have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT people, from the Madras High Court guidelines of 2021 to relief on passport medical examination in February 2026. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 characterises police abuse as limited and non-systemic, which sits alongside documented abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters in 2024 and 2026.

India has an estimated two million transgender people, so the narrowed recognition scheme affects a large population and shapes what a visitor encounters in everyday contact with officials.
localsOnly:
Residents share the national baseline set by the Supreme Court's 2014 third gender ruling, now narrowed by the 2026 amendment for anyone self-identifying outside hijra, kinner or intersex categories. Recognition remains uneven, and discrimination continues in education, healthcare and formal employment.

The government presents the amendment as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. Which schemes a resident can actually reach depends on the medical certification the amendment requires for identity recognition, and on implementation by state authorities in Gujarat.

Residents also live under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, in force since 2024, which dropped the gender-identity-specific offences of the Indian Penal Code; trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code, and the Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines on police sensitisation and conversion therapy bind authorities where they apply.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill was still pending at the time of the March 2026 reporting; whether it has since been granted, and whether implementing rules or forms have been notified, is unresolved in the sources.

No source in the inventory addresses Gujarat specifically. State police conduct, state welfare-scheme implementation, availability of facilities, and any hate-crime data for this state are not sourced, so the absence of a documented deviation should not be read as verified local practice.

The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 reports limited abuse rather than its absence, and its rural-areas qualifier is not tested against urban Gujarat. Whether the 2026 amendment has been challenged in court is not sourced.
